name: Ugali with Sukuma Wiki
summary: Firm white maize porridge served with garlicky, tomato-braised collard greens.
story: Ugali is the everyday staple of Kenya and much of East Africa, eaten with stews, fish or greens. Sukuma wiki, meaning roughly 'push the week' in Swahili, is a cheap sautéed collard dish that helps stretch the household budget.

steps.title: Slice the greens
steps.text: Stack the collard leaves, roll them up and slice as thinly as you can. Rinse and drain well.

steps.title: Fry the onion
steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan and cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic for 1 minute.

steps.title: Add tomatoes
steps.text: Stir in the tomatoes and coriander and cook for 5 minutes until they collapse into a thick sauce.

steps.title: Cook the greens
steps.text: Add the greens in handfuls, stirring until each wilts. Season with salt, cover and cook on medium for 8-10 minutes until tender but still bright green. Finish with lemon.

steps.title: Boil the water
steps.text: While the greens cook, bring 3 cups of the water to a rolling boil in a heavy pot with the salt. Mix the remaining cup of water with a few spoons of the flour to make a thin paste and stir it in.

steps.title: Add the flour
steps.text: Reduce to medium heat and add the maize flour gradually, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, until it begins to thicken into a firm mass with no dry lumps.

steps.title: Cook and press
steps.text: Cover and cook for 3-4 minutes. Then press and fold the ugali against the pot with the spoon for 3-5 minutes until stiff, smooth and pulling cleanly from the sides. It should smell cooked and no longer raw or floury.

steps.title: Shape and serve
steps.text: Wet a bowl, spoon the ugali in, turn it over onto a plate to form a dome. Serve with the sukuma wiki; pinch a piece of ugali, form a scoop and eat the greens with it.

tips: Add the flour slowly while stirring to avoid lumps.
Stir hard; it is a workout, and the vigorous mixing gives a smooth ugali.
Do not overcook the greens or they turn grey and bitter.
Great with nyama choma, fried fish or beef stew.

swaps.swap: Fine white cornmeal (not polenta) or the South African mealie meal; yellow cornmeal works but is coarser and less traditional.
Kale, spring greens or Swiss chard; softer greens need less time.
